name: Optimistic Row
summary: The row appears before the server confirms it, and when the write fails it fails in place — keeping the text, naming the reason, offering retry or discard — instead of vanishing.

attempts.prompt: Add a row optimistically before the server confirms it.
attempts.problem: Appended the row immediately and removed it when the request failed, which is the worst of both approaches: the user sees their entry accepted, looks away, and it silently disappears along with whatever they typed. A rollback the user does not witness is indistinguishable from data loss.

attempts.prompt: Show an error when the write fails instead of removing the row.
attempts.problem: Showed a toast in the corner saying "Failed to save" while the row stayed in its pending state forever. The message named neither which row failed nor why, and offered no way to try again, so the only recovery was a page reload — which loses the entry anyway.

finalPrompt:
Build an optimistic list insert in plain HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript, no dependencies, with a simulated server that fails roughly a third of the time and takes between 500 and 1400 milliseconds.

The row appears the moment the user submits, in a visibly provisional state — reduced opacity and a dashed border — labelled as saving.

The failure path is the component. When the write rejects, the row must fail in place: it stays exactly where it is, keeps the text the user typed, states the reason the server gave, and offers both retry and discard. Never remove the row on failure. A rollback the user does not witness is indistinguishable from losing their data, and it is the single most common way optimistic UI goes wrong.

Never put the failure in a toast. A message elsewhere on the screen cannot say which row failed and disappears before the user can act on it. The error belongs in the row it is about.

Retry must reuse the same row rather than creating a second one, and must return it to the pending state while in flight.

Announce each transition through a role="status" region — saved, failed with the recovery options, discarded — because the visual state change is the only other signal.

Clear the input on submit so the next entry can be typed immediately; the text lives in the row now, and the row is never destroyed.

Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, drop the row entrance animation.

Colour comes only from CSS custom properties: var(--bg), var(--border), var(--text), var(--text-dim), var(--accent), var(--accent-fg), var(--mono). No literal hex, rgb or hsl values.
why:
Optimistic UI is easy to build and easy to build wrong, and both wrong versions appeared here. Removing the row on failure is the intuitive rollback and it is data loss with extra steps. Putting the error in a toast is the intuitive notification and it is unactionable, because by the time the user reads it they cannot tell which of five rows it concerns.

The instruction that produced the right component was naming the invariant: the row is never destroyed. Everything else — keeping the text, the in-place message, retry reusing the same row — follows from it, and none of them had to be specified as separate features.

The general form is worth keeping: for anything optimistic, decide first what happens to the user's input when the optimism turns out to be wrong. That branch is where the trust is won or lost, and it is the branch a happy-path implementation skips.
